sentences.text: Paralititan possessed a robust humerus, or upper arm bone, that measured 1.69 meters in length and featured a large deltopectoral crest.
The tail vertebrae were wider than they were tall and lacked pleurocoels, which are large air-filled spaces found in many other titanosaurs.
Similarly, the sacral vertebrae near the hips also lacked these air-filled spaces.
The scapula, or shoulder blade, possessed a medial concavity bordered by a prominent rugosity, a feature shared with other members of the Titanosauria superfamily.

Paralititan is the first dinosaur confirmed to have inhabited a mangrove habitat, preserved in autochthonous tidal flat deposits containing mangrove vegetation and root marks along the southern shore of the Tethys Sea.
Only 5.1 percent of the skeleton is known, making exact size estimates difficult.
Paralititan was described by American paleontologist Joshua B. Smith and colleagues in 2001 after fossils were found by an American expedition in the Bahariya Oasis, western Egypt.

Researcher Joshua Smith rediscovered the fossil site Gebel el Dist in 1999, where Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf had worked between 1912 and 1914, while a partial sauropod skeleton was found at the nearby site of Gebel Fagga during an expedition.

Recent estimates suggest Paralititan was about 26 meters long and weighed between 30 and 55 tonnes, though American paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter estimated the length at around 26 meters in a 2006 study, Gregory S. Paul estimated the length at over 20 meters and weight at 20 tonnes in his 2010 book, Bernardo González Riga and colleagues estimated the weight at approximately 50 metric tonnes in 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated the weight between 30 and 55 tonnes in 2019, and one estimate suggests it weighed approximately 59 metric tons, because little is known about Paralititan, its exact size is difficult to estimate.

Paralititan is classified as a member of the family Saltasauridae within the superfamily Titanosauria and belongs to the parent group Lithostrotia, which existed during the Cretaceous period on all continents except Australia, and is classified in the class Saurischia, specifically within the subfamily Saltasaurinae, an Afro-European clade alongside Abditosaurus, although Smith and colleagues originally classified it within the now-unused clade Titanosauridae.
Paralititan lived in present-day Egypt during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically in the Bahariya Formation which dates to the Cenomanian stage between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.
It is debated whether several isolated sauropod fossils previously assigned to Aegyptosaurus actually belong to Paralititan.
Researchers suggest that the presence of a large Carcharodontosaurus tooth near the Paralititan skeleton indicates the sauropod was scavenged by the carnivore.
